lessons.label: Activity 6

acts.lead:
Write a two-paragraph editorial.
Paragraph 1:

●   Present your stance on using digital devices instead of textbooks.
●   Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using technology for
learning.

Paragraph 2:

● Choose which is more important (the advantage or the disadvantage)
and explain why.
● Add an example or simple evidence to support your argument.
● End with a strong, persuasive call to action.

Example;

Students should be required to join at least one school club because
clubs provide opportunities to learn, socialize, and develop important skills.
For example, students in a debate club can improve their public speaking and
critical thinking, while students in a sports club learn teamwork and
discipline. Clubs allow students to explore their interests beyond the
classroom, making their school experience more meaningful.
Some may argue that students already have busy schedules with
homework and exams, but joining a club does not need to take too much time.
Schools can offer flexible club schedules so students can balance academics
and activities. Overall, requiring students to join at least one club helps them
grow personally, academically, and socially, preparing them for the future.

items.text: Pick someone in our school whose daily work you don’t fully know — it could be a janitor, cafeteria staff, security guard, teacher, or any support person.

Write at least 6 good questions to interview them. For example: ●    What does a typical workday look like for you here? ●    What part of your job do most students not see? ●    What is something you are proud to have done at this school? ●    What challenges do you face? ●    How did you come to work here? ●    What advice would you give to students?
Arrange and conduct a short interview. Be polite, introduce yourself (“Hi, I’m [Your Name]. I’m writing a feature for class.”), and take notes. If they agree, you can record the conversation.

Use a graphic organizer (or bullet-point notes) to plan your feature: ●    Think about how you will hook your reader (start with a quote, story, or interesting fact) ●    List key details you want to include (their routines, quotes, anecdotes) ●    Plan a closing / reflection: why does their story matter?

Write a 4-paragraph feature article: ●    Paragraph 1 (Lead): Begin with something engaging — a scene, quote, or anecdote. ●    Paragraphs 2–3 (Body): Describe their daily life, their challenges, and what makes them special, using quotes. ●    Paragraph 4 (Conclusion): Reflect on why their story is important to the school community. Example: Title: A Day in the Life of Mrs. Gomez, Our Cafeteria Manager Mrs. Gomez unlocks the cafeteria door at 6:30 a.m., long before most of the students arrive. She pushes a heavy cart filled with trays, cleaning supplies, and fresh bread. “I always like to start early,” she says, smiling. “I want everything to be ready when the kids come in.” By 7:00, she’s already busy: setting up breakfast stations, warming up the ovens, and arranging milk cartons. She hums softly as she works, greeting the first students with a friendly “Good morning!” She knows many of them by name and asks how their morning is going or what they think of the new menu. During lunch, Mrs. Gomez doesn’t just serve food — she listens. A student once told her they didn’t like any sandwiches, so she helped make a special salad just for them. “If I can make someone happy with food, then I feel like I’ve done something good,” she says. She also keeps an eye on the younger kids, making sure they can reach drinks, and helping them open lids when they need it. As afternoon classes begin, she starts cleaning — stacking trays, washing dishes, and sweeping crumbs off the floor. “I don’t just work here to feed students,” she explains. “I work here because I care.” When the cafeteria is quiet again, she takes a moment to look at a small bulletin board where students write thank-you notes. “These reminders make every early morning worth it,” she says. ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ _________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ _________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ _________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________

and fresh bread. “I always like to start early,” she says, smiling. “I want

items.text: Walk around the school or think of places in the school that many people might not notice: a quiet stairwell, a small garden, a forgotten hallway, a storage room, or a maintenance shed.
Spend 5–10 minutes observing your chosen place. Write down: ● What you see, hear, smell, and feel. ● Who uses the place and for what? ● Why this place might be “hidden” or overlooked.

Interview at least one person who knows the place (teacher, staff, or student): ● Ask about memories connected to the place. ● Ask why they go there and what it means to them. ● Ask how the place has changed over time (if it has).
Plan your feature: Use a simple organizer to decide your hook, main observations / quotes, and ending.

lessons.raw:
Instructions:
1. Walk around the school or think of places in the school that many people
   might not notice: a quiet stairwell, a small garden, a forgotten hallway, a
   storage room, or a maintenance shed.
2. Spend 5–10 minutes observing your chosen place. Write down:
              ● What you see, hear, smell, and feel.
              ● Who uses the place and for what?
              ● Why this place might be “hidden” or overlooked.
3. Interview at least one person who knows the place (teacher, staff, or
   student):
              ● Ask about memories connected to the place.
              ● Ask why they go there and what it means to them.
              ● Ask how the place has changed over time (if it has).
4. Plan your feature: Use a simple organizer to decide your hook, main
   observations / quotes, and ending.
5. Write a 3-paragraph article:
              ● Paragraph 1: Describe the place vividly (sensory details,
                setting).
              ● Paragraph 2: Include the interview and what people say
                about the place.
              ● Paragraph 3: Explain why this place matters or what it
                represents.
Sample:
Title: The Quiet Corner by the Art Room
Just outside the art room, hidden behind tall easels and paint-splattered
drop cloths, lies a narrow hallway nook. It’s not a place many students pay
attention to — but if you pause there, you’ll notice it’s special. The walls are
lined with colorful sketches and half-finished canvases. There’s a small
wooden stool where a few students leave their headphones while they paint
or draw.
When I visited, I heard the soft scrape of charcoal against paper and the
steady breathing of someone sketching. The air smelled like turpentine and



resh clay. I saw a few pencil shavings on the floor, and bits of pastel powder
dusted on a nearby shelf.
Ms. Rivera, the art teacher, told me that students sometimes come here
during lunch just to think or make art quietly. “Some of them feel
overwhelmed in class, so this corner gives them space,” she said. She
remembered a student who sat here for a whole lunchtime working on a
self-portrait.
To her, this spot is more than just an empty hallway—it’s a retreat. “It’s
where creativity happens without pressure,” she explained. Even though it's
tucked away, that little corner holds the heart of many students’ artistic
moments.

items.text: Choose an object in our school (or from home) that has meaning: maybe a trophy, an old piece of equipment, a piece of art, a forgotten musical instrument, or something in the staff room.
Research or interview someone about the object: ●   Where did it come from? ●   Who used it? ●   What stories or memories are connected to it? ●   Why is it still kept here?
Examine the object closely: note its color, shape, texture, any marks, age-wear, etc.
Use a planning sheet or graphic organizer to map out: ● A hook (how you will start your story) ● The history / background ● Personal stories / quotes surrounding the object ● A meaningful conclusion

Write a feature-style narrative (3 paragraphs): ●   Paragraph 1: Describe the object in detail so that readers can “see” it. ●   Paragraph 2: Tell the history or the stories linked to it, using interview quotes. ●   Paragraph 3: Reflect on why this object matters — for the school, for people, for memory.
Revise and add a title (e.g., “The Trophy No One Talks About”).

Instructions:
   1. Choose an object in our school (or from home) that has meaning:
      maybe a trophy, an old piece of equipment, a piece of art, a forgotten
      musical instrument, or something in the staff room.
   2. Research or interview someone about the object:
         ●   Where did it come from?
         ●   Who used it?
         ●   What stories or memories are connected to it?
         ●   Why is it still kept here?
   3. Examine the object closely: note its color, shape, texture, any marks,
      age-wear, etc.
   4. Use a planning sheet or graphic organizer to map out:
             ● A hook (how you will start your story)
             ● The history / background
             ● Personal stories / quotes surrounding the object
             ● A meaningful conclusion


   5. Write a feature-style narrative (3 paragraphs):
         ●   Paragraph 1: Describe the object in detail so that readers can
             “see” it.
         ●   Paragraph 2: Tell the history or the stories linked to it, using
             interview quotes.
         ●   Paragraph 3: Reflect on why this object matters — for the
             school, for people, for memory.
   6. Revise and add a title (e.g., “The Trophy No One Talks About”).
   7. If possible, take a photo or draw the object and include it with your
      article.
Example:
Title: The Old School Bell That Never Rung
In the back storage room, tucked away on a dusty wooden shelf, sits a large,
round brass bell. It’s dulled from years of neglect, and the once-shiny



surface is covered in patches of dark green tarnish. The label reads: “School
Bell — Class of 1978.” No longer hung in the hallway or rung during
assemblies, it feels like a forgotten piece of school history.
Mr. Delacruz, a retired teacher, remembers when the bell used to ring.
“Every Monday morning,” he recalled, “a student would pull the rope to call
everyone together for the weekly assembly.” He smiled as he told me how
students used to joke about ringing the bell just to skip class — but no one
ever dared.
Over time, the school built a new PA system, and the bell stopped being
used. But alumni still ask about it when they come back. Some touch the
brass gently, others snap photos. “It’s more than just a bell,” said Mr.
Delacruz. “It’s a symbol of our school’s past — of days when things were
simpler.”
Now, the bell stays silent, but it continues to have meaning. For former and
current students, it reminds them of generations who walked these halls, of
their shared memories, and of the passage of time.

acts.lead:
Activity 1. Identify the parts of column writing

Headline                       Body                     Opinion
Conclusion                     Introduction

________1. In conclusion, introducing mindfulness exercises at school is a
simple yet effective way to support students’ mental health and learning.
Even a few minutes each day can have lasting positive effects on their
overall well-being.

________2. Mindfulness is the practice of being fully aware of the present
moment and noticing thoughts, feelings, and surroundings without
judgment. Studies show it can reduce stress, enhance focus, and help
students cope with the demands of school life.

_______3. Mindfulness in Schools: Improving Focus and Well-Being.

_______4. Students who practice mindfulness techniques such as deep
breathing, meditation, or journaling report lower stress levels and increased
concentration. Teachers observe improved behavior, more participation in
class, and a calmer classroom atmosphere. Mindfulness also encourages
emotional awareness and empathy, which strengthens relationships with
peers.

_______5. I believe all students should incorporate mindfulness into their
daily routines because it promotes calmness, mental clarity, and better
focus. Developing this skill early can improve both emotional well-being and
academic performance.

acts.lead:
“Citizens Protest Over Corruption in Flood-Control Projects”

In 2025, many Filipinos are deeply worried about corruption in the
government. Reports have emerged that billions of pesos meant for flood-
control infrastructure — projects to prevent flooding — may have been
misused. Wikipedia+2The Diplomat+2
Some of these projects are allegedly “ghost” projects — meaning the money
was spent, but the actual construction was never finished or was done very
poorly. Wikipedia Because of this, many people think these mismanaged
flood-control systems make flooding worse instead of better. Wikipedia
Public dissatisfaction grew, and on September 21, 2025, a huge number of
people protested in Luneta Park (Manila) and other cities. This protest is
called the “Trillion Peso March”, and it demands transparency,
accountability, and changes in how government funds are handled.
Wikipedia+2Wikipedia+2
The protests reflect a growing concern: corruption is now one of the top
issues for Filipinos, according to recent surveys.
BusinessMirror+2Philstar+2 Business groups have also joined the calls for
reform, saying that corruption hurts ordinary people and weakens
institutions. The Diplomat

Draw a cartoon that captures the mass protest during the “Trillion Peso
March.” They should highlight:
●   People united in protest (students, church groups, citizens)
●   Signs or placards (e.g., “Transparency,” “Stop Corruption,” “Where’s
the Flood Money?”)
●   A river or flood scene in the background, symbolizing the flood-control
projects under fire
●   A building labeled “Government / DPWH / Congress” to symbolize the
authorities being held accountable
